processing: A way of preparing tea, not a factory style. Green tea, mainly from the Cangshan area, is roasted in a heated clay pot over charcoal with constant shaking until slightly yellow and fragrant, then boiling water goes in and the pot rumbles and crackles.
harvest_season: Not tied to a harvest: it is made at the table from whatever local green tea the host has.
appearance_dry: Ordinary local green tea, turned slightly yellow and toasted in the pot.
appearance_wet: Darkened, toasted leaves left at the bottom of the pot.
taste_profile: Bitter and toasty with a cooling edge and a mellow finish; it is meant to be the hard opening of the three courses.

brewing.notes: Warm a small clay pot, roast the leaf while shaking until it smells toasted and turns slightly yellow, then add a little boiling water. Let the foam settle, top up, wait briefly and pour. Take care, as the pot spits.

vintage_note: Not sold as a product or by year. It is prepared on the spot from local green tea, so what matters is that the leaf is fresh enough to roast cleanly. Current-year green tea is the sensible choice.
description:
Leixiang, thunder tea, is the first and bitter cup of the Bai three-course tea of Dali. It is named for the noise the pot makes when boiling water hits the hot roasted leaf.

The host warms an empty clay pot, adds green tea and shakes it over charcoal until the leaf yellows slightly and smells toasted. The shaking goes on long enough to earn it a second name, hundred-shake tea. A splash of boiling water sets off the rumble, the foam settles, and the pot is topped up.

Expect a strong, bitter, toasted cup in orange to amber, served in a small amount. It is not meant to be pleasant in the way of a fine green. The bitterness is the point, standing for the hard start of a life in the sequence of bitter, sweet and aftertaste.

The second course sweetens things with brown sugar and walnut, and the third brings honey with Sichuan pepper and cinnamon. Recipes vary from house to house. To try it at home, use an inexpensive green tea and a small clay pot you do not mind scorching.
history:
Thunder tea belongs to the Bai three-course tea custom, a hospitality ritual of Dali listed as Chinese intangible cultural heritage. Little is documented about thunder tea as a separate drink, and it has no date or maker of its own.

Details of the recipe differ between tellings.
